limitations: Study 1: Relatively small sample for two conditions (29 people), effects not strong, no baseline data collected, even density of two persons per m² is high and not common in everyday life, social situations mediate comfort, time had an unexpected effect (adaptation), group composition (gender) not considered.

Study 2: Data subject to sequence effects, increased cognitive effort due to masks (COVID-19 pandemic) affecting emotion recognition, no decisive explanation for communication effect (possibly chance finding).

Study 3: Pure laboratory study, results not transferable to one-to-one real life, subjects not intrinsically motivated to be fast or under deadline pressures, physical exertion had a significant effect on skin conductance.

Study 4: Only distance to people in front and behind considered, not left and right, no subjective perceptions measured after each condition, distinction between near and far zones in walking questioned.

General: EDA method is difficult to use, susceptible to motion artifacts and environmental factors, artifact detection is complex, signal recording and electrode contact problems lead to data loss and subject exclusion.
General: HR sensors also show high subject dropout due to artifact-laden data (over 50% loss in Studies 2, 3, 4), HR is highly susceptible to physical arousal/exertion.
General: Experimental designs may be influenced by specific expectancies.

General: Field observations require good scripts to capture individual experience, high logistical effort for trajectory cameras, cameras do not capture all environmental information (sounds, atmosphere), need for interviews to attribute arousal to specific violations.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the relationship between pedestrian density, walking speed, and psychological stress, using electrodermal activity (EDA) and subjective ratings. Across four studies, it was found that while waiting in dense situations, subjective discomfort increased with density, but physiological arousal showed complex, context-dependent patterns, suggesting adaptation over time and mediation by social factors like communication. In contrast, when pedestrians were moving, increased density (and associated reduced walking speed) consistently led to increased physiological arousal. Faster walking speeds also increased arousal, attributed to physical exertion and higher cognitive load during free navigation. The research provides empirical evidence for the Pedestrian Level of Service (PLOS) assumption that stress increases with density, particularly when moving. Limitations include small sample sizes in some studies, potential sequence effects, the controlled laboratory setting limiting real-life generalizability, and the inherent challenges of isolating specific stressors with physiological measures like EDA.
